---
title: Mid-Term Project Specifications
---

## Overview

This project seeks to build out an agentic AI solution for finding grants.gov solicitations and building teams of VT faculty from the College of Science (CoS) that could apply for, receive funding, and implement an effective research program. For now, the solution is limited to CoS but should extend to other VT colleges (for interdisciplinary solicitations).

## Requirements & Resources

1. The application should query the REST API from grants.gov to pull currently open solicitations from all programs. Closed solicitations can be archived but should not be shown to the user. This application is about building teams for net-new solicitations, not managing the research portfolio.
2. [`authors.csv.zip`](authors.csv.zip) contains a list of CoS faculty with important metrics (such as the H5 index). This file was generated through work done by the VT library. There is a VT website, but it is not made available to students (at this time).
3. [`publications.csv.zip`](publications.csv.zip) contains all the research publications for CoS faculty members (including abstracts). This file was sourced from the Elsevier API (all VT students have access to the API via an API key they generate). Initial prototypes can use the `.csv` file, but the final product should use the API directly.
4. Teams generated by the tool must be reproducible, explainable, and rational (i.e. easily defended), based on a holistic understanding of publications and faculty metrics. This is a non-trivial ask!

## Use Cases

1. A user should be able to pull the latest grants.gov solicitations (update the local database). Then the user should be able to filter/sort the solicitations by type, date, amount, etc.
2. The user should be able to select a solicitation and click a button to `build a team`.
3. After a user clicks `build a team`, they should be transferred to a chatbot interface (with RAG) that automatically builds a team based on a user-defined prompt template + RAG content.
4. The user can follow up on this initial generation.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-midterm-flow
%%| fig-cap: "The main user flow. The user refreshes and filters solicitations, picks one, and clicks build-a-team; that hands off to a RAG/GraphRAG chatbot that retrieves faculty evidence and proposes an explainable team the user can refine through follow-up turns."
sequenceDiagram
    participant User as "User"
    participant UI as "Streamlit UI"
    participant Grants as "grants.gov API"
    participant Store as "Local DB"
    participant Bot as "Team-building chatbot"
    participant Retr as "RAG / GraphRAG"
    User->>UI: refresh solicitations
    UI->>Grants: search2 (open statuses)
    Grants-->>Store: open solicitations (archive closed)
    User->>UI: filter / sort, select one
    User->>UI: click "build a team"
    UI->>Bot: solicitation + prompt template
    Bot->>Retr: retrieve faculty publications + metrics
    Retr-->>Bot: ranked evidence
    Bot-->>User: proposed team with rationale
    User->>Bot: follow-up (swap member, adjust scope)
    Bot-->>User: revised team
```

## Deliverables

- A working Streamlit application implementing the use cases above (refresh/filter solicitations → build-a-team chatbot with conversational follow-up).
- The **[Requirements & Architecture write-up](../../assignments/mid_term_project_reqs_and_arch.qmd)** — a separate 500-point exercise, due **W5 · C2 (Sep 24)**, before you build. It is where you answer the *Questions for Consideration* below, enumerate the requirements, name the LLM/RAG issues each one exposes, and argue the architecture, the level of agency it earns, and the pattern that mitigates each issue. **No AI assistance on that document.**
- A short design section in your README that carries the same argument forward into the delivered code: your retrieval choice (RAG vs. GraphRAG vs. hybrid) and how team recommendations are made reproducible, explainable, and rational.
- Python source code with descriptive in-line comments, and instructions to run the app (including the expected `.env` keys).

### What you submit, and when

The mid-term has **two parts**:

1. **[Requirements & Architecture write-up](../../assignments/mid_term_project_reqs_and_arch.qmd)** — due **W5 · C2 (Sep 24)**.
2. **Source zip + video run-through** — due at the **end of Week 9 (Fri Oct 23)**, submitted together on Canvas:
   - **A `.zip` of your project source** — the code, a README with run instructions and the expected `.env` keys, and any data files your app needs. Do **not** include your `.env`; it holds your API keys.
   - **A screen-recorded video run-through** of your solution working end to end: refresh and filter solicitations, build a team for one, and ask a follow-up question in the chatbot. If you don't have a recording tool, use the free, open-source [OBS Studio](https://obsproject.com).

There is no live presentation. The instructor also unzips, runs, and tests your source, so it must work by following your README. Week 8 classes are virtual (Panopto video on Canvas) so you have time to finish the build.

## Rubric

The project is scored out of **1000 points**.

| Category | What we're looking for | Points |
|---|---|---:|
| grants.gov integration | Pulls open solicitations via the REST API; archives closed ones; supports filter/sort | 150 |
| Faculty data integration | Uses `authors.csv` / `publications.csv` (or, better, the Elsevier API) with metrics like H5 index | 100 |
| Retrieval (RAG / GraphRAG) | A working ChromaDB and/or Neo4j retrieval layer over publications and metadata | 150 |
| Team-building chatbot | Build-a-team handoff, prompt template + retrieved context, conversational follow-up | 200 |
| Team quality | Recommendations are reproducible, explainable, rational, and holistic | 150 |
| Streamlit front-end | Usable, responsive UI covering the full solicitation → team flow | 100 |
| Design write-up & justification | Addresses the *Questions for Consideration*; justifies retrieval and design choices | 75 |
| Code quality & in-line comments | Readable, well-structured code with descriptive comments and run instructions | 75 |
| **Total** | | **1000** |

: {tbl-colwidths="[26,58,16]"}

## Questions for Consideration

1. What is an optimal team?
2. What is the parsimonious (agentic or not) design to implement this solution?
3. RAG or GraphRAG?
4. What are the LLM and RAG limitations that might make our teams non-optimal?
5. How do we generate optimal teams using LLMs and RAG? There are many limitations we must overcome. Can we address them with agentic design patterns?
6. How do we balance generation costs with optimal outcomes?

## Links

The application depends on the following external APIs and services, grouped by role: **data sources** (grants + publications), the **LLM providers** that power the RAG chatbot, and the **graph database** backing GraphRAG. Each entry includes documentation and, where applicable, API-key signup.

### 1. Grants.gov REST API — solicitations

Public and **unauthenticated** — the search/fetch endpoints accept anonymous POST requests. (A key, obtained via a Help Desk ticket, is only needed for grantor/applicant system-to-system integrations, which this project does not use.) Two endpoints are likely relevant:

| Resource | Link |
|---|---|
| API Guide (start here) | <https://www.grants.gov/api/api-guide> |
| API Resources overview | <https://www.grants.gov/api> |
| `search2` — list/search opportunities | <https://grants.gov/api/common/search2> — `POST https://api.grants.gov/v1/api/search2` |
| `fetchOpportunity` — full detail (award amounts, synopsis) | `POST https://api.grants.gov/v1/api/fetchOpportunity` (see API Guide) |
| Opportunity detail page (human-readable link) | `https://www.grants.gov/search-results-detail/{oppId}` |
| Simpler.Grants.gov API (modernized REST API + OpenAPI) | <https://wiki.simpler.grants.gov/product/api> |

**Example request (no auth):**

```bash
curl --location 'https://api.grants.gov/v1/api/search2' \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"keyword": "biology", "oppStatuses": "forecasted|posted"}'
```

Filter on `oppStatuses` (`forecasted|posted` for open work); archive anything `closed`/`archived` rather than displaying it.

### 2. Elsevier / Scopus APIs — faculty publications & abstracts

`publications.csv` was sourced from Elsevier. For the production version, query the API directly. All VT students can generate a free API key on the Elsevier Developer Portal. **Note:** abstract/full-text access and quotas depend on VT's subscription, so run requests from the campus network (or with an institutional token) to receive entitled content. Two endpoints are likely relevant — Scopus Search (find publications by author ID / affiliation) and Abstract Retrieval (per-publication abstract + index keywords):

| Resource | Link |
|---|---|
| Elsevier Developer Portal (home) | <https://dev.elsevier.com/> |
| **Sign in / create account to get an API key** | <https://dev.elsevier.com/user/signin> |
| Manage / create API keys | <https://dev.elsevier.com/apikey/manage> |
| Scopus API Getting Started Guide (PDF) | <https://dev.elsevier.com/guides/Scopus%20API%20Guide_V1_20230907.pdf> |
| Scopus Search API — `GET https://api.elsevier.com/content/search/scopus` | <https://dev.elsevier.com/documentation/ScopusSearchAPI.wadl> |
| Abstract Retrieval API — `GET https://api.elsevier.com/content/abstract/scopus_id/{id}` | <https://dev.elsevier.com/documentation/AbstractRetrievalAPI.wadl> |
| Author Retrieval API (alternate source of h-index / author metrics) | <https://dev.elsevier.com/documentation/AuthorRetrievalAPI.wadl> |
| API interface specifications (all endpoints) | <https://dev.elsevier.com/api_docs.html> |
| API support | apisupport@elsevier.com |

**Key signup steps:** create a free account → "Create API Key" → supply a label and a website URL (a personal site is fine) → agree to the terms of service. Quotas reset on a rolling 7-day window, and each key is tied to one application.

### 3. VT UDC Research Metrics portal — faculty roster & metrics

`authors.csv` (faculty roster plus h-index, citation counts, collaboration %, etc.) is sourced from VT's University Data Commons (UDC), accessed behind CAS single sign-on — this is a gated VT portal, not a public REST API.

| Resource | Link |
|---|---|
| UDC Research Metrics | <https://udc.vt.edu/research_impact/data/research_metrics/index> |
| VT CAS login (SSO) | <https://login.vt.edu/profile/cas/login> |

### 4. LLM provider — VT ARC hosted LLMs

The RAG chatbot will use the **hosted VT ARC LLMs**. These are OpenAI-compatible endpoints provided by VT's Advanced Research Computing. See <http://ads1.datasci.vt.edu/ai_research/coding/vt_ai.html> for how to request an API key.

- **Endpoint:** `https://llm-api.arc.vt.edu/api/v1`
- **Default model:** `vt-arc-llm`

Store the API key and endpoint URL in a `.env` file (never commit it):

```bash
# .env
VT_ARC_API_KEY=sk-arc-3f9aZ1exampleKeyDoNotUse8b2c7d
VT_ARC_BASE_URL=https://llm-api.arc.vt.edu/api/v1
VT_ARC_MODEL=vt-arc-llm
```

| Resource | Link |
|---|---|
| VT ARC AI / API key instructions | <http://ads1.datasci.vt.edu/ai_research/coding/vt_ai.html> |

### 5. RAG / GraphRAG database

The chosen retrieval approach drives the database:

- **RAG (vector search):** **ChromaDB** is a strong option — embed faculty publication abstracts and metadata, then retrieve by semantic similarity. Runs locally (no API key) with a simple Python client or a persistent server.
- **GraphRAG:** **Neo4j** is a strong option for modeling faculty, departments, publications, and keyword/collaboration relationships explicitly, queried via Cypher (no API key — local Bolt connection, run via Docker).

A hybrid of both is also viable. See the *Questions for Consideration* above ("RAG or GraphRAG?").

| Resource | Link |
|---|---|
| ChromaDB docs | <https://docs.trychroma.com/> |
| Neo4j download / Docker image | <https://neo4j.com/download/> |
| Cypher query language docs | <https://neo4j.com/docs/cypher-manual/current/> |
| Neo4j Python driver | <https://neo4j.com/docs/python-manual/current/> |
